def: Training a model to give the probability of each possible next token given the tokens before it, which defines a distribution over whole sequences by the chain rule.
The average negative log probability that the model gave to the true next token, minimised during language-model training.
Choosing the weights that make the training text as probable as possible under the model, which is the same as minimising cross-entropy.
The function that turns a vector of logits into probabilities by exponentiating each entry and dividing by the sum.
The exponential of the average loss in nats: the number of equally likely options the model is, on average, as unsure among.
The total information the model needs per byte of original text, a unit that stays comparable across different tokenisers.
The unit of information measured with the natural logarithm; one nat is about 1.44 bits.
Training with the true previous tokens as input at every position, rather than the model's own earlier predictions.
Excluding some positions, such as padding or the prompt, from the loss by an ignore index, so only the remaining positions contribute.
A count-based language model that predicts the next token from the previous n minus one tokens using frequencies in the training text.
The negative log probability of a token that actually occurred, in bits or nats: how surprised the model was.
Scoring each token with as much context as the model allows by moving a fixed-length window forward in small strides and scoring only its last positions.
